content: This extensive judgment from the Court of Ascoli Piceno Civil Section addresses complex claims between former spouses concerning the legal community property regime and deferred community of income from separate activities. The plaintiff requested the defendant pay €388,500 overall, claiming it falls within matrimonial community property comprising half of €211,144.24 obtained from successful labor lawsuit, half of severance pay received as teacher, and return of sums withdrawn from joint current account during marriage. The defendant contested and counterclaimed for return of half of plaintiff's professional income and business profits not proven to be used for family purposes. The central issue concerned whether sums owed to the defendant for professional services rendered between 1979 and 1992 during the marriage but judicially recognized only in 2009 by labor court judgment (after dissolution of community in 1996) fall within legal community property pursuant to Article 177(c) of the Italian Civil Code. The court extensively reviewed Supreme Court jurisprudence, particularly Cassation judgment 5797/2006, which held that income from separate activities of spouses does not automatically enter immediate community but remains property of respective owner until dissolution, entering only for the part not consumed at that moment. The court held that Article 177(c) establishes deferred community (community of remainder) taking place at dissolution, limited to what actually exists in individual spouse's assets, not what could have been found therein. Income from separate activity consumed prior to dissolution, even for personal purposes, is excluded from legal community. The receiving spouse has full power of enjoyment, administration and disposal over income from personal activity pursuant to Article 217 of the Civil Code, subject only to obligation to contribute to family needs. No legally protected right exists for either spouse over the other's income and its administration. The deferred community creates simple de facto expectation, not real credit right, with real transfer effected only at dissolution. In the specific case, at dissolution the defendant did not have the sums now claimed, as labor court recognition occurred only in 2009 after separation and divorce. Even if sums related to services during marriage, had they been paid regularly the defendant could have disposed of them freely, and no presumption exists they would remain available at dissolution or that they were consumed to detriment of family rather than for its benefit. Including sums recognized in 2009 in community dissolved in 1996 would attribute all-encompassing nature exceeding legal provisions. The court also rejected claims regarding severance pay and account withdrawals as time-barred, noting they should have been addressed in separation/divorce proceedings. The defendant's counterclaim was similarly rejected as time-barred. All claims were rejected and costs fully compensated given lack of unanimity on legal nature of deferred community institution.
